name: Gallium
blurb: Gallium is never observed in vivo by NMR, but 68Ga from a benchtop 68Ge/68Ga generator is one of the most used PET nuclides in oncology (PSMA-11, DOTATATE), so it is a constant presence in PET/MR. Its two stable isotopes are both spin 3/2 and are well behaved solid-state NMR probes of aluminosilicate and nitride frameworks.
mrNotes: 68Ga has a 68 min half-life and an 89% positron branch, and is eluted from a 68Ge/68Ga generator, so a PET/MR site can produce it without an on-site cyclotron.
71Ga is the preferred observe isotope: 1.27 times the gamma of 69Ga and a Q of 10.7 fm2 against 17.1 fm2, so its quadrupolar broadening is roughly 2.5 times smaller.
PET tracer mass doses are nanomolar, so 68Ga radiopharmaceuticals cause no measurable susceptibility artifact in a simultaneous MR acquisition.

isotopes.notes: Solid-state workhorse for distinguishing 4-coordinate Ga (about +100 to +250 ppm) from 6-coordinate Ga (about -30 to +60 ppm) in gallosilicates and GaN.
Higher gamma and smaller Q than 69Ga; resonates at 122 MHz on a 400 MHz (9.4 T) spectrometer. The preferred Ga nucleus in almost every application.
SPECT agent (67Ga citrate) for infection and lymphoma imaging, largely displaced by 18F-FDG. Nuclear moment not reliably tabulated; left null.
Positron emitter for PET; not an NMR nucleus. Ground state is 1+ but the magnetic moment is not reliably tabulated, so mu, gamma and Q are left null here.

name: Germanium
blurb: 73Ge is the least receptive stable nucleus in routine use, about 0.64 times 13C despite being 7.75% abundant, because its gyromagnetic ratio is only -1.49 MHz/T. Germanium's only real contact with an imaging department is 68Ge, the generator parent that supplies 68Ga for PET.
mrNotes: 73Ge resonates at 14.0 MHz on a 400 MHz spectrometer, low enough that probe and preamp noise, not sample concentration, often set the detection limit.
I = 9/2 with Q = -19.6 fm2: lines in non-cubic sites are broad, and most published spectra are of tetrahedrally symmetric organogermanes.
68Ge (271 d) is the long-lived parent in 68Ga generators and is also the standard sealed source for PET scanner normalization and phantom work.

isotopes.notes: The only NMR-active Ge isotope. Receptivity 0.64 relative to 13C; long acquisitions and symmetric sites are essential. GeCl4 sits at +31 ppm, GeH4 at -285 ppm, GeI4 near -1080 ppm.

name: Arsenic
blurb: 75As is 100% abundant with a healthy gamma of 7.32 MHz/T, but a quadrupole moment of 31.1 fm2 means that anything less symmetric than AsF6- or AsO4 3- is broadened out of existence. It has no in vivo MR application.
mrNotes: Second-order quadrupolar broadening of the central transition scales as 1/B0, so 75As is one of the nuclei that gains most from moving to the highest available field.
Arsenic exposure and speciation in tissue are measured by ICP-MS and XAS, not by NMR.
Arsenic trioxide is a standard therapy in acute promyelocytic leukaemia, but it is invisible to every MR method.

isotopes.notes: Q = 31.1 fm2 (Pyykko 2018, revised down from the older 31.4 fm2 muonic value). Only high-symmetry species such as AsF6-, AsO4 3- and As(CH3)4+ give observable lines, so no representative shift range is quoted.

name: Selenium
blurb: 77Se is the workhorse chalcogen NMR nucleus: spin 1/2, 7.6% abundant, receptivity about 3 times 13C, and a shift range near 3500 ppm that makes it a sensitive reporter of selenium coordination. Despite selenocysteine and selenoproteins being biologically central, 77Se has not been observed in vivo.
mrNotes: Natural-abundance 77Se spectra are routine on a broadband probe; at 9.4 T it sits at 76.5 MHz, just below 13C.
Relaxation is dominated by chemical shift anisotropy, so T1 lengthens at high field and recycle delay, not sensitivity, usually limits the experiment.
77Se enrichment is commercially available and is the usual route into selenoprotein NMR; in vivo detection has never been demonstrated.

isotopes.notes: Caution for reference tables: many compilations still list mu = 0.5350 muN and gamma/2pi = 8.157 MHz/T, which are inconsistent with the measured Xi = 19.0715 by 0.45%, far more than any plausible shielding correction. The 2025 shielding-corrected redetermination gives mu = 0.53380(3) muN and gamma/2pi = 8.138 MHz/T, used here. Secondary reference (PhSe)2 at +463 ppm.

name: Bromine
blurb: Both bromine isotopes are spin 3/2 with quadrupole moments near 30 fm2, so observation is confined to the free bromide ion and a few cubic solids. Bromide is present in plasma at roughly 50 micromolar and has never been imaged.
mrNotes: 81Br is the better nucleus: 1.08 times the gamma of 79Br and a 16% smaller Q, giving about 0.7 times the quadrupolar relaxation rate for the same field gradient.
Bromide relaxation, not chemical shift, was the classical observable; 81Br T2 was used in the 1970s to probe anion binding sites in serum albumin and carbonic anhydrase.
Brominated compounds are common in anaesthetics and flame retardants but contribute no MR signal and no susceptibility artifact at physiological concentrations.

isotopes.notes: Q = 31.3 fm2 (Pyykko, revised from the older 33.1 fm2). Resonates at 100.6 MHz at 9.4 T, essentially on top of 13C, which is a practical nuisance on broadband probes.
Preferred Br isotope: higher gamma, smaller Q, and nearly the same abundance as 79Br. Q = 26.2 fm2 (Pyykko, revised from 27.6 fm2).

name: Krypton
blurb: 83Kr is the third hyperpolarizable noble gas after 3He and 129Xe, and the only one whose quadrupole moment is the point. Because I = 9/2 with Q = 25.9 fm2, hyperpolarized 83Kr relaxes on contact with a surface, so its T1 reports directly on alveolar surface-to-volume ratio rather than on chemical shift.
mrNotes: SQUARE (surface quadrupolar relaxation) contrast has been demonstrated in excised and in vivo rodent lungs, including a rat elastase model of emphysema.
gamma/2pi is only -1.644 MHz/T, so 83Kr sits at 4.9 MHz at 3 T and 2.5 MHz at 1.5 T, which requires a purpose-built low-frequency coil and preamplifier.
SEOP polarization for 83Kr reaches a few percent, well short of the tens of percent routine for 129Xe, and gas-phase T1 is seconds rather than minutes, so the polarizer must sit next to the subject.
Natural krypton is only 11.5% 83Kr; isotopic enrichment buys close to a factor of 9 in signal and is standard for imaging work.

isotopes.notes: mu = -0.9707297(32) muN from the 2014 gas-phase redetermination against 3He, more precise than the older -0.970669. Chemical shift is not the useful observable in lung imaging; quadrupolar T1, of order 1 to 2 s in vivo, is.

name: Rubidium
blurb: Rubidium is the vapour that polarizes everything else. Rb metal at 100 to 200 C pumped with 795 nm circularly polarized light transfers electron spin polarization to 129Xe, 3He or 83Kr by spin exchange, which is how essentially every clinical hyperpolarized gas dose is made.
mrNotes: SEOP cells run Rb number densities of order 1e14 per cm3; a cold trap and filter remove residual Rb before the gas is dispensed for inhalation.
87Rb (I = 3/2) is the isotope of the optical-pumping and atomic-magnetometer literature; 85Rb (I = 5/2) is the more abundant at 72.2%. Either works for spin exchange.
82Rb (75 s, from a 82Sr/82Rb generator) is the standard cardiac perfusion PET tracer, so rubidium appears on both the MR and the PET side of a PET/MR suite.
87Rb NMR has followed Rb+ as a potassium analogue in perfused hearts and excised tissue; there is no established in vivo human application.

isotopes.notes: The abundant isotope. I = 5/2 with Q = 27.6 fm2; in solution Rb+ shifts span only a few ppm, so solid-state work dominates.
Effectively stable (beta- to 87Sr, the basis of Rb-Sr geochronology). Highest receptivity of the two, about 290 times 13C. Solid-state 87Rb isotropic shifts span roughly 150 ppm across common salts.
Cardiac perfusion PET tracer eluted from a 82Sr generator; a potassium analogue taken up by myocytes. Not an NMR nucleus; moment not tabulated here.

name: Strontium
blurb: 87Sr is one of the harder nuclei in the periodic table: gamma/2pi of only -1.85 MHz/T, spin 9/2, and Q = 30.5 fm2, giving a receptivity of about 1.1 times 13C at 7% abundance. Strontium reaches the clinic through nuclear medicine rather than MR.
mrNotes: Only near-cubic Sr sites give tractable 87Sr lineshapes; lower symmetry broadens the central transition past usefulness below about 18 T.
Strontium substitutes for calcium in hydroxyapatite, which is why 89Sr (50.6 d, pure beta) localizes to osteoblastic bone metastases for pain palliation.
82Sr (25.4 d) is the generator parent for 82Rb cardiac PET.

isotopes.notes: Stable, and the radiogenic daughter of 87Rb. Detection generally needs very high field or DNP; no representative solution shift range is quoted because so few species have been measured.
Pure beta emitter (1.49 MeV) used for bone pain palliation in osteoblastic metastases. Not an NMR nucleus; moment left null.

name: Yttrium
blurb: 89Y is spin 1/2 at 100% natural abundance, which sounds ideal until you see gamma/2pi = -2.09 MHz/T, the smallest of any stable spin 1/2 nucleus. The upside is T1 values of minutes, which has made hyperpolarized 89Y chelates an unusually slow-decaying DNP probe. Clinically, yttrium means 90Y radioembolization.
mrNotes: 89Y T1 in solution can exceed 5 minutes, so DNP-hyperpolarized 89Y complexes survive far longer than hyperpolarized 13C; demonstrations so far are in solution and phantoms, not in vivo.
At 3 T the 89Y Larmor frequency is 6.3 MHz, below the tuning range of most clinical broadband hardware.

90Y (64.0 h, pure beta, 2.28 MeV endpoint) is used for hepatic radioembolization and in ibritumomab tiuxetan; the glass or resin microspheres are not MR-visible and are localized by bremsstrahlung SPECT or 90Y PET.
86Y (14.7 h) is the positron-emitting surrogate used for pre-therapy 90Y dosimetry.

isotopes.notes: Receptivity 0.70 relative to 13C: 100% abundance barely compensates for the tiny gamma. T1 of minutes makes long recycle delays or a relaxation agent mandatory. Y2O3 gives resonances at +271 and +314 ppm.
Positron emitter used as the imaging surrogate for 90Y dosimetry. Moment not tabulated here.
Therapeutic pure beta emitter for radioembolization. Ground state is 2-; the magnetic moment is not reliably tabulated for a reference table and is left null.

name: Zirconium
blurb: 91Zr is a low-gamma spin 5/2 nucleus that is essentially a solid-state NMR speciality. Zirconium's real presence in an imaging department is zirconia ceramic in dental and hip components, which is non-magnetic and artifact-free, and 89Zr for antibody PET.
mrNotes: 89Zr has a 78.4 h half-life that matches the days-long biodistribution of monoclonal antibodies, which is why it dominates immuno-PET.
Yttria-stabilized zirconia femoral heads and dental crowns produce no susceptibility artifact; any artifact in the image comes from the metal stem or post they sit on.
91Zr is 11.2% abundant with gamma/2pi = -3.97 MHz/T and Q = -17.6 fm2; almost all reported spectra are static or MAS solid state rather than solution.

isotopes.notes: Receptivity about 6.3 times 13C. Quadrupolar broadening dominates and reported work is mostly solid-state (zirconocenes, zirconates); no representative solution shift range is quoted.
Immuno-PET nuclide, produced by 89Y(p,n). Ground state 9/2+; magnetic moment measured but not reliably tabulated for reference use, so left null.

name: Niobium
blurb: Niobium is the metal that makes the magnet. Every clinical scanner carries its persistent current in NbTi wire, superconducting below 9.2 K, and the highest-field NMR magnets use Nb3Sn at 18.3 K. 93Nb is also a superb NMR nucleus, 100% abundant with receptivity about 2900 times 13C, but it is never seen in vivo.
mrNotes: NbTi (Tc 9.2 K) is the conductor in essentially all 1.5 T and 3 T magnets at 4.2 K; 7 T systems push it harder, the 11.7 T Iseult magnet runs NbTi at 1.8 K, and NMR magnets above about 18 T require Nb3Sn (Tc 18.3 K).
A 3 T whole-body magnet stores several MJ; if a normal zone nucleates in the NbTi winding, that energy lands in the helium, which is the quench the vent pipe exists for.
93Nb has the largest magnetic moment in this slice at +6.17 muN and I = 9/2, so despite being quadrupolar (Q = -32 fm2) it is one of the most receptive nuclei in the periodic table.

isotopes.notes: Receptivity roughly 2900 times 13C, second only to 1H and a few others among common nuclei. Resonates at 98.2 MHz at 9.4 T, close enough to 13C to matter on a broadband probe. Niobate site assignments: 4-coordinate about -650 to -950 ppm, 6-coordinate about -900 to -1360 ppm.

name: Molybdenum
blurb: Molybdenum reaches magnetic resonance through hardware and through the isotope supply chain: molybdenum permalloy is a standard magnetic shielding alloy, and 99Mo is the generator parent of 99mTc, which is most of nuclear medicine. Both NMR-active isotopes are low-gamma spin 5/2 nuclei.
mrNotes: Molybdenum permalloy (about 4% Mo, 79% Ni, balance Fe) shields photomultipliers, magnetometers and cabling near the fringe field of a scanner.
95Mo is the isotope to observe: Q is only -2.2 fm2 against +25.5 fm2 for 97Mo, so its quadrupolar relaxation rate is more than 100 times lower at nearly identical gamma.
99Mo (65.9 h) generators supply the 99mTc used for bone, cardiac and renal SPECT; a reactor outage is felt in the nuclear medicine schedule within days.
Molybdenum is a trace element in xanthine oxidase and sulfite oxidase, but the tissue concentration is orders of magnitude below any MR detection threshold.

isotopes.notes: Preferred Mo nucleus. The very small Q of -2.2 fm2 gives surprisingly narrow lines for a spin 5/2 metal. Mo(CO)6 sits at -1857 ppm, thiomolybdates well above +2000 ppm.
Marginally higher gamma than 95Mo but a Q more than 10 times larger, so lines are far broader. Rarely used.
Fission-produced parent of 99mTc in the technetium generator. Ground state 1/2+; magnetic moment not reliably tabulated, left null.
